chapter: Decca records, the Savoy and Moe Gale
title: Moe Gale, Chicago, Gary and the Paradise Theatre in Detroit
summary: Tim Gale heard the band at Gary, Indiana on the way east; their first theatre date at Detroit's Paradise was a hit, especially Hibbler and Walter Brown.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: The success of the blues, would that have been partly responsible for Moe Gale wanting you to go to the Savoy -- how come that you went --

Well, I wouldn't say that was primarily the whole cause. I think it was because we went to the Savoy, he sent his brother out, Tim Gail to hear the band at Gary, Indiana, and we were on our way to New York.
Yeah, we had played Chicago and we played Gary.
Where did you play in Chicago?
What was the name of that ballroom.
A place on 43rd and S. Park.

There was a little old place where teenagers used to come in there. Oh, I can't even think of that, but I remember it was 43rd. We played there in Chicago and then we went to Gary, and played Gary and then went from Gary, our first theatre date, to Paradise in Detroit; and incidentally, they're trying to revive the Paradise in Detroit, because the guy called me up and wanted to know if I'd come down there and they had about a 16-piece band there and they wanted me to come in there and headline one night, one Sunday afternoon which would be about the 7th of January. They said they were trying
to get it started again, but that was my first theatre date I ever played in my life there in Detroit at the Paradise Theatre, so we went into the Paradise --
Yes, we had to play the show.
So that was a new experience for you.

That was a new experience, but the thing about it, the people just went crazy over - well, first of all, they went crazy over Hibler, but I always brought Hibler on first and the people, they just broke up -- you know what I mean, s- then we'd have the comedy and whatever else down there and then I'd bring Walter Brown on and they'd go crazy again, which was beautiful, and Walter Brown was singing the blues, you know, and they did like the blues there in Detroit.

So that our first experience it was nice, and of course, I didn't know whether it was going to be like that or not. We had been a few places like down in Texas and a few places in the South where they liked the blues but we didn't get that reaction like that until after we went back, after the record was out. But in Detroit they went right all for it.
I guess they had a lot of southern people in Detroit then during the war, didn't they.
